{{Short description|Field of study in physics}}
In [[physics]], '''generalized hydrodynamics''' (GHD) is an extension of ordinary [[Fluid dynamics|hydrodynamics]] to [[Non-equilibrium thermodynamics|non-equilibrium]] [[Integrable system|integrable]] systems. Such systems have a large number of [[Conserved quantity|conserved quantities]], leading to hydrodynamics with infinitely many [[conservation law]]s.<ref name=ehiiqs>{{cite journal
 | last1=Castro-Alvaredo | first1=Olalla A.
 | last2=Doyon           | first2=Benjamin
 | last3=Yoshimura       | first3=Takato
 | title=Emergent Hydrodynamics in Integrable Quantum Systems Out of Equilibrium
 | journal=Physical Review X
 | volume=6
 | issue=4
 | article-number=041065
 | year=2016
 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.6.041065
 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevX.6.041065
}}</ref> In ordinary hydrodynamics, there exists only a limited amount of conservation laws for [[energy]], [[mass]] and [[momentum]].

Generalized hydrodynamics started out from the need to model [[Non-equilibrium thermodynamics|non-equilibrium]], but still integrable systems (both quantum and classical).

The equations of GHD are collisionless [[Boltzmann equation]]s for the stable quasi particle excitations of integrable systems.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1=Doyon             | first1=Benjamin
 | last2=Gopalakrishnan    | first2=Sarang
 | last3=Møller            | first3=Frederik
 | last4=Schmiedmayer      | first4=Jörg
 | last5=Vasseur           | first5=Romain
 | title=Generalized Hydrodynamics: A Perspective
 | journal=Physical Review X
 | volume=15
 | issue=1
 | article-number=010501
 | year=2025
 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevX.15.010501
 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevX.15.010501
}}</ref> So unlike ordinary hydrodynamics, that is prone to [[Thermalisation|thermalization]] (no information of microscopic movement is being kept of), GHD keeps track of all information during the dynamical evolution of the system.

GHD is a relatively new field of study, having evolved from two papers in 2016,<ref name=ehiiqs />
<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1=Bertini     | first1=Bruno
 | last2=Collura     | first2=Mario
 | last3=De Nardis   | first3=Jacopo
 | last4=Fagotti     | first4=Maurizio
 | title=Transport in Out-of-Equilibrium XXZ Chains: Exact Profiles of Charges and Currents
 | journal=Physical Review Letters
 | volume=117
 | issue=20
 | article-number=207201
 | year=2016
 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.207201
 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.117.207201
}}</ref> although some examples of integrable systems such as [[Lieb–Liniger model]] describing cold atomic gasses in one dimension satisfying the [[Bose–Einstein statistics|Bose-Einstein statistics]] were considered in 1963.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1=Lieb     | first1=Elliott H.
 | last2=Liniger  | first2=Werner
 | title=Exact Analysis of an Interacting Bose Gas. I. The General Solution and the Ground State
 | journal=Physical Review
 | volume=130
 | pages=1605–1616
 | year=1963
 | doi=10.1103/PhysRev.130.1605
}}</ref> The [[Bethe ansatz]] can be seen as a starting point of GHD.

Applications of GHD span from interacting integrable quantum systems, spin transport, quantum dynamics of propagating waves in interacting Bose gases, soliton gases to classical molecular dynamics.

==General framework==
===The main equation===
Generalized hydrodynamics is for now restricted to one-dimensional problems. In such settings, many-body systems display the notion of integrability and the emergent Euler-scale hydrodynamics becomes generalized hydrodynamics instead of classical hydrodynamics.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1 = Bonnemain
 | first1 = Thibault
 | last2 = Caudrelier
 | first2 = Vincent
 | last3 = Doyon
 | first3 = Benjamin
 | title = Hamiltonian formulation and aspects of integrability of generalised hydrodynamics
 | journal = Journal of Physics A: Mathematical and Theoretical
 | year = 2019
 | volume = 52
 | issue = 14
 | page = 144001
 | doi = 10.1088/1751-8121/ab07e0
}}</ref>

The central equation of GHD closely resembles both the [[Euler equations (fluid dynamics)|Euler equations]] of fluid dynamics and the [[Liouville's theorem (Hamiltonian)#Liouville equation|Liouville equation]]. It takes the form of a nonlinear integro-differential equation governing the quasiparticle spectral phase-space distribution <math>\rho_{\lambda}</math>, given by:

<math>\partial_t \rho_{\lambda} + \partial_x \left(v^{\text{eff}} \rho_{\lambda}\right)=0,</math>

where <math>\rho_{\lambda}(x,\lambda ,t)</math> is the density of quasiparticles which depends on space, spectral parameter <math>\lambda</math> (also called rapidity) and time. The effective velocity <math>v^{\text{eff}}(x,\lambda, t)</math> is the velocity of the propagation of the excitations of quasiparticles and depends nonlinearly on the <math>\rho_{\lambda}</math>, i.e. it depends nontrivially on the interactions.

If contributions from force fields are included than the equations take the form:

<math>\partial_t \rho_{\lambda} + \partial_x \left(v^{\text{eff}} \rho_{\lambda}\right)+\partial_{\lambda}\left(a^{\text{eff}}\rho_{\lambda}\right)=0</math>.

The continuous spectral parameter <math>\lambda</math> enumerates
the possible asymptotic objects of the interactions between particles (scattering theory, solitons, etc.), including their momentum and possible internal states. The precise set of <math>\lambda</math> dependts on the model but is usually either <math>\mathbb R</math> or some subset <math>S \in \mathbb R</math>. That way, the particles become quasiparticles that now live in ''spectral phase space''.

For a system of non-interacting particles the ''spectral phase space'' becomes the regular [[phase space]], the spectral parameter becomes the canonical momentum <math>\lambda \rightarrow p</math> and the equation of motion becomes the single particle Liouville equation:

<math>\partial_t \rho + \dot{x}\,\partial_x \rho + \dot{p}\,\partial_p \rho = 0,</math>

or equivalently

<math>\partial_t \rho + \{\rho, H\} = 0,</math>

with the usage of [[Hamilton's equations]] and [[Poisson bracket]]s.

The GHD equations are usually solved numerically<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1=Bastianello    | first1=Alvise
 | last2=Alba           | first2=Vincenzo
 | last3=Caux           | first3=Jean-Sébastien
 | title=Generalized hydrodynamics with space-time inhomogeneous interactions
 | journal=Physical Review Letters
 | volume=123
 | article-number=130602
 | year=2019
 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.123.130602
 | url=https://link.aps.org/doi/10.1103/PhysRevLett.123.130602
}}</ref> but the equations themselves have integrable structures and are prone to geometric descriptions from which solutions in terms of a set of integral equations can be obtained.<ref>{{cite journal
 | last1=Doyon     | first1=Benjamin
 | last2=Spohn     | first2=Herbert
 | last3=Yoshimura | first3=Takato
 | title=A geometric viewpoint on generalized hydrodynamics
 | journal=Nuclear Physics B
 | volume=926
 | pages=570–595
 | year=2018
 | doi=10.1016/j.nuclphysb.2017.12.018
 | url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S055032131730677X
}}</ref>

===Integrable systems and relaxation time===
Classical hydrodynamics is based on the assumption that the [[relaxation time]] (time needed for a perturbed system to come to [[Thermodynamic equilibrium|equilibrium]]) of particles is much smaller than the time scale of macroscopic changes, i.e. <math>\tau_{\text{micro}} \ll \tau_{\text{macro}}</math>, so that we do not need to track every particle's position and momentum <math>(q_i,p_i)</math> simultaneously but we only need to keep track of [[Bulk property|bulk properties]] like [[density]] <math>\rho(\mathbf{r},t)</math>, [[velocity]] <math>v(\mathbf{r},t)</math> and [[energy density]] <math>e(\mathbf{r},t)</math> and the whole evolution can be described with a [[Navier–Stokes equations|set of PDE's]] and only those few conserved quantities.

The situation is different in GHD, here the relaxation time is not negligible and the assumption of relaxation can not be used as easily as in classical hydrodynamics.

A conserved quantity <math>Q</math> with the appropriate density <math>q(x)</math> can be expressed as

<math>Q = \int dx q(x),</math>

One can now write down <math>n</math> conservation laws ([[continuity equation]]s) for each conserved quantity of the form:

<math>\partial_t q_n+\partial_x j_n=0.</math>

Usually, [[Hamiltonian system|Hamiltonian]] integrable systems have a finite number of conserved quantities (namely the Hamiltonian, momentum, angular momentum).
The special property of GHD systems is that the number of independent conserves quantities grows linearly with the system's size. Another distinction is that a non-integrable system that is set to evolve starting from a non-equilibrium state it will approach a statistical ensemble the [[Canonical ensemble|Gibbs ensemble]], while the integrable system will evolve to the ''generalized Gibbs ensemble'':

<math>\rho = \frac{e^{\sum \beta_n Q_n}}{Z}</math>

where <math>{Q_n}</math> is an infinite family of conserved quantities and <math>\beta_n</math> are generalized chemical potentials.

===Non-equilibrium states===
In theory, non-equilibrium statistical mechanics is mathematically exact: ensembles for an isolated system evolve over time according to deterministic equations such as Liouville's equation or its quantum equivalent, the [[von Neumann equation]]. These equations are the result of applying the mechanical equations of motion independently to each state in the ensemble. These ensemble evolution equations inherit much of the complexity of the underlying mechanical motion, and so exact solutions are very difficult to obtain. Moreover, the ensemble evolution equations are fully reversible and do not destroy information (the ensemble's [[Gibbs entropy]] is preserved).
